platforms.title: Why Is Your Cough Still Hanging On Weeks After a Cold?
platforms.meta_description: A cough that outlasts your cold by weeks is common and usually harmless. Here is why it lingers, what the NHS says helps, and when it is time to see a GP.
platforms.body_html:
The fever broke days ago, your nose has stopped running, and you feel mostly fine. Yet every night the tickle comes back, and a dry, hacking cough interrupts conversations at work. If this sounds familiar, you are in very good company. The NHS says a cough will usually clear up on its own within 3 to 4 weeks, and NICE guidance for doctors (NG120) describes acute cough the same way: self-limiting, most often caused by a viral infection such as a cold or flu, and getting better without antibiotics. The catch is that "3 to 4 weeks" feels like forever when you are the one coughing.

What keeps a cough going after the virus has left

A cough is a reflex, not a disease. Nerve endings in the lining of your throat and airways fire whenever something irritates them, and your chest muscles respond by forcing air out. During a cold, the virus inflames that lining. When the infection clears, the lining stays sensitive for a while, so ordinary triggers like cold air, talking or lying down are enough to set the reflex off. That is why the cough often outlives every other symptom.

The NHS lists several other things that commonly keep a cough going, and more than one can overlap with the tail end of a cold. One is mucus dripping down the throat from the back of the nose, which keeps tickling the same nerves even after you stop feeling congested. Others include smoking, heartburn (acid reflux) and allergies such as hay fever. Infections like bronchitis or COVID-19 can also leave a cough behind. Reassuringly, the NHS adds that a cough is rarely a sign of something serious like lung cancer.

Smoke deserves a special mention because it is the one trigger you can usually remove today. Cigarette smoke irritates exactly the lining that is trying to recover, so smoking, or sitting in a smoky room, can stretch a post-cold cough out well beyond the usual few weeks.

3 Things That Actually Help a Lingering Cough

1. Try hot lemon and honey. The NHS suggests squeezing half a lemon into a mug of boiled water and adding 1 to 2 teaspoons of honey, drunk while still warm. NICE lists honey as a self-care option with limited evidence of some benefit for people aged over 1 year. Never give honey to babies under 1, and do not give hot drinks to small children.

2. Use pharmacy remedies for relief, not a cure. A pharmacist can suggest cough syrups, cough medicines or cough sweets. The NHS is clear that these will not stop your cough, though they may help you cough less. Decongestants and cough medicines containing codeine will not stop it either, and some products should not be given to children under 12. A herbal medicine called pelargonium is an option for people aged 12 or over, although the NHS notes the evidence for herbal remedies is limited.

3. Rest, drink plenty of fluids and cut out smoke. These are the NHS's first-line self-care steps. Keeping a drink by your bed helps when a night-time tickle starts, and staying away from cigarette smoke gives irritated airways a chance to settle. If you have a high temperature or do not feel well enough for normal activities, try to stay at home and avoid contact with other people.

You Don't Have to Treat Every Cough

Antibiotics are not normally prescribed for coughs, because most are caused by viruses. A GP will only prescribe them if you need them, for example for a bacterial infection or if you are at risk of complications. Waiting it out is a genuine treatment plan for most post-cold coughs, not a lack of one.

There are clear limits, though. The NHS advises seeing a GP if you have had a cough for more than 3 weeks, if you are losing weight for no reason, or if you have a weakened immune system, for example because of chemotherapy or diabetes. Ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111 if your cough is very bad or getting worse quickly, if you have chest pain, find it hard to breathe, feel very unwell, have a swollen and painful side of the neck, or are coughing up blood. At the appointment, a GP may listen to your chest, test a mucus sample, or arrange an X-ray or a lung function test.

If you remember just one thing, make it this: a cough past the 3-week mark is the point to stop waiting and book a GP, even if you otherwise feel fine. Until then, honey, fluids, rest and a smoke-free home are the most useful things you can do. This article is general health information and does not replace advice from your doctor.

Sources: NHS, "Cough" (page reviewed December 2023); NICE guideline NG120, "Cough (acute): antimicrobial prescribing".
